claim: Drosophila cortex glia are restricted to brain regions devoid of synapses.
source: Drosophila cortex glia are restricted to brain regions devoid of synapses, providing an opportunity to characterize interactions with neuronal somas.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characteristic of Drosophila cortex glia.

claim: Mutations in the cortex glial NCKXzydeco elevate basal Ca2+.
source: Mutations in the cortex glial NCKXzydeco elevate basal Ca2+, predisposing animals to seizure-like behavior.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mutations in NCKXzydeco predispose animals to seizure-like behavior.
source: Mutations in the cortex glial NCKXzydeco elevate basal Ca2+, predisposing animals to seizure-like behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through behavioral assays in the results.

claim: Elevation of glial Ca2+ causes hyperactivation of calcineurin-dependent endocytosis.
source: We show that elevation of glial Ca2+ causes hyperactivation of calcineurin-dependent endocytosis and accumulation of early endosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by CalexA reporter data and Rab5 imaging experiments.

claim: Elevation of glial Ca2+ causes accumulation of early endosomes.
source: We show that elevation of glial Ca2+ causes hyperactivation of calcineurin-dependent endocytosis and accumulation of early endosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by Rab5::GFP imaging showing increased large Rab5-positive puncta in zyd cortex glia.

claim: Knockdown of sandman recapitulates NCKXzydeco seizures.
source: Knockdown of sandman, a K2P channel, recapitulates NCKXzydeco seizures.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by behavioral seizure assays with sandman RNAi.

claim: Sandman expression on cortex glial membranes is substantially reduced in NCKXzydeco mutants.
source: Indeed, sandman expression on cortex glial membranes is substantially reduced in NCKXzydeco mutants, indicating enhanced internalization of sandman predisposes animals to seizures.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immunofluorescence and Western blot data showing reduced SAND:GFP levels in zyd.

claim: Enhanced internalization of sandman predisposes animals to seizures.
source: Indeed, sandman expression on cortex glial membranes is substantially reduced in NCKXzydeco mutants, indicating enhanced internalization of sandman predisposes animals to seizures.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the reduced sandman expression data.

claim: A single astrocytic glia contacts multiple neuronal cell bodies, hundreds of neuronal processes, and tens of thousands of synapses.
source: A single astrocytic glia contacts multiple neuronal cell bodies, hundreds of neuronal processes, and tens of thousands of synapses (Halassa et al., 2007; Ventura and Harris, 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Cultured astrocytes oscillate intracellular Ca2+ spontaneously.
source: Cultured astrocytes oscillate intracellular Ca2+ spontaneously (Takata and Hirase, 2008) and in response to neurotransmitters (Agulhon et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2010), including glutamate (Cornell-Bell et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Cultured astrocytes oscillate intracellular Ca2+ in response to neurotransmitters.
source: Cultured astrocytes oscillate intracellular Ca2+ spontaneously (Takata and Hirase, 2008) and in response to neurotransmitters (Agulhon et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2010), including glutamate (Cornell-Bell et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Glutamate released during normal synaptic transmission is sufficient to induce astrocytic Ca2+ oscillations.
source: Glutamate released during normal synaptic transmission is sufficient to induce astrocytic Ca2+ oscillations (Dani et al., 1992; Wang et al., 2006), which trigger Ca2+ elevation in co-cultured neurons (Nedergaard, 1994; Parpura et al., 1994) that can elicit action potentials (Angulo et al., 2004; Fellin et al., 2006; Fellin et al., 2004; Pirttimaki et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Astrocytic Ca2+ oscillations trigger Ca2+ elevation in co-cultured neurons.
source: Glutamate released during normal synaptic transmission is sufficient to induce astrocytic Ca2+ oscillations (Dani et al., 1992; Wang et al., 2006), which trigger Ca2+ elevation in co-cultured neurons (Nedergaard, 1994; Parpura et al., 1994) that can elicit action potentials (Angulo et al., 2004; Fellin et al., 2006; Fellin et al., 2004; Pirttimaki et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Astrocyte-induced Ca2+ elevation in neurons can elicit action potentials.
source: Glutamate released during normal synaptic transmission is sufficient to induce astrocytic Ca2+ oscillations (Dani et al., 1992; Wang et al., 2006), which trigger Ca2+ elevation in co-cultured neurons (Nedergaard, 1994; Parpura et al., 1994) that can elicit action potentials (Angulo et al., 2004; Fellin et al., 2006; Fellin et al., 2004; Pirttimaki et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Increased glial activity is associated with abnormal neuronal excitability.
source: Indeed, increased glial activity is associated with abnormal neuronal excitability (Wetherington et al., 2008), and pathologic elevation of glial Ca2+ can play an important role in the generation of seizures (Gómez-Gonzalo et al., 2010; Tian et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Pathologic elevation of glial Ca2+ can play an important role in the generation of seizures.
source: Indeed, increased glial activity is associated with abnormal neuronal excitability (Wetherington et al., 2008), and pathologic elevation of glial Ca2+ can play an important role in the generation of seizures (Gómez-Gonzalo et al., 2010; Tian et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The Drosophila CNS contains two specialized astrocyte-like glial subtypes that interact specifically either with dendrites and synapses (astrocytes) or with neuronal cell bodies (cortex glia).
source: Drosophila provides an ideal system to study glial-neuronal soma interactions as the Drosophila CNS contains two specialized astrocyte-like glial subtypes that interact specifically either with dendrites and synapses (astrocytes, Stork et al., 2014) or with neuronal cell bodies (cortex glia, Awasaki et al., 2008; Pereanu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Cortex glia encapsulate all neuronal cell bodies in the CNS with fine, lattice-like processes.
source: Cortex glia encapsulate all neuronal cell bodies in the CNS with fine, lattice-like processes (Awasaki et al., 2008; Coutinho-Budd et al., 2017) (Figure 1A) and are thought to provide metabolic support and electrical isolation to their neuronal counterparts (Buchanan and Benzer, 1993; Volkenhoff et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Cortex glia are thought to provide metabolic support and electrical isolation to neurons.
source: Cortex glia encapsulate all neuronal cell bodies in the CNS with fine, lattice-like processes (Awasaki et al., 2008; Coutinho-Budd et al., 2017) (Figure 1A) and are thought to provide metabolic support and electrical isolation to their neuronal counterparts (Buchanan and Benzer, 1993; Volkenhoff et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: There are no apparent morphological changes in cortex glial wrapping of neuronal soma in zyd mutants compared to wildtype.
source: Immunofluorescence imaging reveals no apparent morphological changes in cortex glial wrapping of neuronal soma (3rd instar larval brains, magenta: anti-Elav, neuronal nuclei; green: anti-GFP, mCD8:GFP, cortex glial membrane).
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1A and shown in the immunofluorescence images.

claim: Cortex volume occupied by cortex glial processes shows no difference between wildtype and zyd.
source: Quantification of cortex volume occupied by cortex glial processes shows no difference between wildtype and zyd (n > 15 brains for each genotype, p=0.138).
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1B and shown in the quantification graph.

claim: Cortex glial cell body surface area shows no difference between wildtype and zyd.
source: Quantification of cortex glial cell body surface area shows no difference between wildtype and zyd (n > 120 cells/ N = 4 animals for each genotype, p=0.0892).
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1C and shown in the quantification graph.

claim: Cortex glial processes between neuronal cell bodies are as thin as 50 nm in both wildtype and zyd.
source: Electron microscopy images of cortex glial contacts (arrowheads) with neuronal somas (N). Cortex glial processes between neuronal cell bodies are as thin as 50 nm in both wildtype and zyd.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1D and shown in the electron microscopy images.

claim: Chronic or conditional knockdown of zyd with cortex glial drivers reproduces the zyd mutant seizure phenotype.
source: Time course of Heat-shock induced seizures (38.5°C, HS) following chronic or conditional knockdown of zyd with two different cortex glial drivers (NP2222 and GMR54H02) is shown. Rearing adult flies at the restrictive temperature (>30°C) for gal80ts (a temperature-sensitive form of the gal4 inhibitor, gal80, see Materials and methods) removes gal80 inhibition of gal4 and allows expression of zydRNAi only at the adult stage. These manipulations reproduce the zyd mutant seizure phenotype (N = 4 groups of 20 flies/genotype).
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1E and shown in the behavioral data.

claim: Larval and adult seizures in zyd mutants have similar temperature threshold and kinetics.
source: Behavioral analysis of HS-induced seizures at 38.5°C shows that larval and adult seizures have similar temperature threshold (F) and kinetics (G) (N = 4 groups of 10–20 animals/condition/treatment).
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1F-G and shown in the behavioral data.

claim: The voltage required to induce seizures in zyd is not significantly different from wildtype.
source: Seizure thresholds in wildtype, zyd and Parabss1 (positive control) are shown. The voltage required to induce seizures in zyd is not significantly different from wildtype (35.32 ± 3.65V and 31.33 ± 2.12V, p=0.3191, n ≥ 7 flies/genotype).
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1H and shown in the electrophysiology data.

claim: Neuronal knockdown of cac rescues the zyd seizure phenotype.
source: Behavioral analysis of the time course of HS-induced seizures indicates neuronal knockdown of cac (C155>cacRNAi) rescues the zyd seizure phenotype. Inset shows results after 1 minute of HS (p=0.0004, N = 4 groups of 20 flies/genotype).
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1I and shown in the behavioral data.

claim: Wildtype cortex glia exhibit small, rapid Ca2+ oscillations.
source: In vivo Ca2+ imaging using a myristoylated Ca2+ sensitive-GFP (myrGCaMP5) revealed small, rapid cortex glial Ca2+ oscillations in wildtype Drosophila larvae (Figure 1—video 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by imaging data.

claim: Zyd mutants lack microdomain Ca2+ transients and exhibit elevated baseline intracellular Ca2+.
source: In contrast, zyd mutants lack microdomain Ca2+ transients and exhibit elevated baseline intracellular Ca2+ (Figure 1—video 3), indicating altered glial Ca2+ regulation underlies seizure susceptibility in zyd mutants (Melom and Littleton, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by imaging data and citation.

claim: No change in cleaved DCP1 levels were found in zyd mutants, indicating basal cell death was unaffected.
source: To determine if loss of ZYD affected glial or neuronal cell survival, we quantified the cell death marker DCP-1 (cleaved death caspase protein-1 [Akagawa et al., 2015]) in control and zyd 3rd instar larvae and adults. No change in cleaved DCP1 levels were found, indicating basal cell death was unaffected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Western blot data.

claim: Wildtype, zyd and NP2222>zydRNAi larvae exhibited similar frequencies of type I and type II responses in the gentle touch assay.
source: We found that wildtype, zyd and NP2222>zydRNAi larvae exhibited similar frequencies of type I and type II responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: Adult zyd flies exhibited normal locomotion at room temperature.
source: In addition, adult zyd flies exhibited normal locomotion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) and larvae exhibited normal light avoidance responses at room temperature (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), indicating baseline neuronal properties required for these behaviors are unaffected.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: Zyd larvae exhibited normal light avoidance responses at room temperature.
source: In addition, adult zyd flies exhibited normal locomotion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) and larvae exhibited normal light avoidance responses at room temperature (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), indicating baseline neuronal properties required for these behaviors are unaffected.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: Pan-neuronal knockdown of Cacophony significantly reduced locomotion and rescued zyd TS-induced seizures.
source: Pan-neuronal knockdown of Cacophony (cac), the presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channel responsible for neurotransmitter release (Kawasaki et al., 2004; Rieckhof et al., 2003), significantly reduced locomotion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) and rescued zyd TS-induced seizures (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data and citations.

claim: Pan-glial knockdown of CanB2 completely rescued both heat-shock and vortex induced seizures in zyd animals.
source: In the RNAi screen for zyd interactors, pan-glial knockdown of the regulatory calcineurin (CN) B subunit, CanB2, completely rescued both heat-shock and vortex induced seizures in zyd animals (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: Recordings from zyd;;repo >CanB2RNAi#1 larvae exhibit normal rhythmic firing at 38°C similar to wildtype controls.
source: Recordings of the motor central pattern generator (CPG) muscle output at the larval neuromuscular junction (NMJ), showed that in contrast to the continuous neuronal firing observed in zyd mutants, recordings from zyd;;repo >CanB2RNAi#1 larvae exhibit normal rhythmic firing at 38°C similar to wildtype controls (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: The zyd seizure phenotype was partially rescued when combined with a heterozygous CanB2 knockout allele.
source: In addition, the zyd seizure phenotype was partially rescued when combined with a heterozygous CanB2 knockout (zyd;CanB2KO/+) allele (Nakai et al., 2011; Figure 2A, CanB2KO homozygotes are lethal and could not be tested).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data and citation.

claim: CanB2 knockdown in astrocytes resulted in no rescue of the zyd phenotype.
source: CanB2 knockdown in astrocytes resulted in no rescue of the zyd phenotype, while CanB2 knockdown with a cortex-glial specific driver (NP2222-gal4) greatly improved the zyd phenotype (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: CanB2 knockdown with a cortex-glial specific driver greatly improved the zyd phenotype.
source: CanB2 knockdown in astrocytes resulted in no rescue of the zyd phenotype, while CanB2 knockdown with a cortex-glial specific driver (NP2222-gal4) greatly improved the zyd phenotype (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: Cortex glial-specific knockdown of CanB2 using two copies of the CanB2 RNAi construct resulted in ~90% of zyd;NP2222>CanB22xRNAi adult animals lacking seizures.
source: Rescue was greatly enhanced by cortex glial-specific knockdown of CanB2 using two copies of the CanB2 RNAi construct (Figure 2E, Figure 2—video 3), with ~90% of zyd;NP2222>CanB22xRNAi adult animals lacking seizures.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: Adult flies conditionally expressing CanB2RNAi exhibited significantly fewer seizures after 3 days, with only ~20% of flies displaying zyd-like seizures by 5 days.
source: Adult flies reared at the permissive temperature for gal80ts (>30 ˚C) to allow CanB2RNAi expression exhibited significantly fewer seizures after 3 days, with only ~20% of flies displaying zyd-like seizures by 5 days (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: Pan-glial knockdown of two CanA subunits, Pp2B-14D and CanA-14F, partially rescued zyd heat-shock and vortex-induced seizures.
source: We found that pan-glial knockdown of two CanA subunits, Pp2B-14D and CanA-14F, partially rescued zyd heat-shock and vortex-induced seizures (Figure 2B,G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: Rescue was enhanced by knockdown of both Pp2B-14D and CanA-14F, with more than ~90% of zyd;;repo>Pp2B-14DRNAi,CanA-14FRNAi flies lacking seizures.
source: Rescue was enhanced by knockdown of both Pp2B-14D and CanA-14F (Figure 2H), with more than ~90% of zyd;;repo>Pp2B-14DRNAi,CanA-14FRNAi flies lacking seizures, suggesting a redundant function of these two subunits in glial cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: Overexpressing Pp2B-14DH217Q resulted in ~50% of zyd/Pp2B-14DH217Q flies becoming seizure-resistant regardless of the driver used.
source: We next overexpressed a dominant negative form of CanA (Pp2B-14DH217Q) using either pan-glial (repo-gal4) or two different cortex-glial specific drivers (NP2222-gal4 and GMR54H02-gal4). Overexpressing Pp2B-14DH217Q resulted in ~50% of zyd/Pp2B-14DH217Q flies becoming seizure-resistant regardless of the driver used (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: CN knockdown had no effect on wildtype cortex glial Ca2+ oscillatory behavior or the elevated basal Ca2+ levels and the lack of microdomain Ca2+ events in zyd cortex glia.
source: Imaging intracellular Ca2+ in cortex glia with GMR54H02-gal4 driving myrGCaMP6s revealed that CN knockdown had no effect on wildtype cortex glial Ca2+ oscillatory behavior or the elevated basal Ca2+ levels and the lack of microdomain Ca2+ events in zyd cortex glia (Figure 2J–K, Figure 2—video 4 and 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by imaging data.

claim: CN function is required downstream of elevated intracellular Ca2+, rather than to regulate Ca2+ influx or efflux in cortex glial cells.
source: These observations indicate CN function is required downstream of elevated intracellular Ca2+, rather than to regulate Ca2+ influx or efflux in cortex glial cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the Ca2+ imaging data.

claim: A substantial basal activation of CN was observed in control 3rd instar larval cortex glia at room temperature.
source: A substantial basal activation of CN was observed in control 3rd instar larval cortex glia at room temperature using fluorescent imaging (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by CalexA imaging data.

claim: CN activity and the resulting GFP expression was enhanced in zyd cortex glia.
source: CN activity and the resulting GFP expression was enhanced in zyd cortex glia (Figure 3B) and greatly reduced in zyd/CanB2RNAi cortex glia (Figure 3C–C').
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by CalexA imaging data.

claim: Western blot analysis revealed enhanced cortex glial CN activity in adult zyd mutants compared to controls (23 ± 3% enhancement).
source: Western blot analysis of CalexA-induced GFP expression in adult head extracts revealed enhanced cortex glial CN activity in adult zyd mutants compared to controls (23 ± 3% enhancement, Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Western blot data.

claim: RNAi knockdown of CanB2 reduced CalexA GFP expression by 27 ± 1%.
source: RNAi knockdown of CanB2 reduced CalexA GFP expression as expected (27 ± 1%, Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Western blot data.

claim: Zyd flies fed with 1 mM CsA for 12 hr showed ~80% fewer seizures than controls.
source: Zyd flies fed with 1 mM CsA for 12 hr showed ~80% fewer seizures than controls (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: Seizure rescue by CsA was dose-dependent.
source: Seizure rescue by CsA was dose-dependent, with less robust suppression when flies were fed with 0.3 mM CsA (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: The CsA rescue was reversible, as seizures reoccurred following 12 hr of CsA withdrawal.
source: The CsA rescue was reversible, as seizures reoccurred following 12 hr of CsA withdrawal (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: Feeding flies with FK506 resulted in a partial rescue of the zyd phenotype.
source: Feeding flies with a second anti-CN drug, FK506, resulted in a partial rescue of the phenotype (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: Pan-glial knockdown of sandman caused adult flies to undergo TS-induced seizures similar to zyd mutants.
source: This screen revealed that pan-glial knockdown of sandman (sand), the Drosophila homolog of TRESK (KCNK18) and a member of the two-pore-domain K+ channel family (K2P), caused adult flies to undergo TS-induced seizures similar to zyd mutants (Figure 5A, Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: TS-induced seizures in repo>sandRNAi adults were found to have the same kinetics and temperature threshold as seizures observed in zyd mutants.
source: TS-induced seizures in repo>sandRNAi adults were found to have the same kinetics and temperature threshold as seizures observed in zyd mutants (Figure 5A,B), and CPG recordings showed that repo>sandRNAi larvae exhibit rapid, unpatterned firing at 38°C, similar to zyd (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral and electrophysiology data.

claim: Repo>sandRNAi larvae exhibit rapid, unpatterned firing at 38°C, similar to zyd.
source: TS-induced seizures in repo>sandRNAi adults were found to have the same kinetics and temperature threshold as seizures observed in zyd mutants (Figure 5A,B), and CPG recordings showed that repo>sandRNAi larvae exhibit rapid, unpatterned firing at 38°C, similar to zyd (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: Cortex-glial specific knockdown of sand recapitulated ~50% of the seizure effect when two copies of the RNAi were expressed.
source: Cortex-glial specific knockdown of sand recapitulated ~50% of the seizure effect when two copies of the RNAi were expressed (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: Inhibition of CN by RNAi or CsA did not alter sandRNAi-induced seizures, placing sand downstream of CN activity.
source: Indeed, inhibition of CN by RNAi or CsA did not alter sandRNAi-induced seizures (Figure 5F), placing sand downstream of CN activity.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: Knockdown of sand in the zyd background does not alter the elevated basal Ca2+ or the lack of microdomain Ca2+ events in zyd mutants.
source: Furthermore, knockdown of sand in the zyd background does not alter the elevated basal Ca2+ or the lack of microdomain Ca2+ events in zyd mutants (Figure 5G,H), and cortex glial Ca2+ oscillatory behavior in repo >sandRNAi is similar to wildtype (Figure 5G,H and Figure 5—video 2), suggesting sand is downstream to the abnormal Ca2+ signaling in zyd.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by imaging data.

claim: SAND:GFP expression is reduced by ~45% when both sand and sandRNAi are expressed using a pan glial driver.
source: First, we used these lines to verify sand knockdown by sandRNAi, and found that SAND:GFP expression is reduced by ~45% when both sand and sandRNAi are expressed using a pan glial driver (repo-gal4), while the expression of a control RNAi did not change SAND:GFP expression (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Western blot data.

claim: SAND:GFP is not differentially phosphorylated in zyd relative to wildtype cortex glia.
source: We found that SAND:GFP was not differentially phosphorylated in wildtype versus zyd mutants (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Phos-tag gel data.

claim: SAND:GFP is phosphorylated on several phosphorylation sites in cortex glia.
source: Multiple bands were detected when samples were pre-treated with alkaline phosphatase (Figure 6C, arrowheads), indicating SAND:GFP is indeed phosphorylated on several phosphorylation sites in cortex glia.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Phos-tag gel data.

claim: SAND:GFP fluorescence is reduced by 53 ± 6.85% in zyd cortex glia.
source: Indeed, examination of SAND:GFP distribution within cortex glial cells showed a significant reduction in SAND:GFP fluorescence on cortex glial membranes (53 ± 6.85% reduction, Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: SAND:GFP expression level was reduced by ~34 ± 15% in zyd cortex glia.
source: Consistent with this observation, SAND:GFP expression level detected by western blot analysis was reduced by ~34 ± 15% in zyd cortex glia (Figure 6F–G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Western blot data.

claim: No difference was detected in membrane tethered GFP (mCD8:GFP) expressed in wildtype and zyd cortex glia.
source: The reduction in expression was specific to sand, and not due to a general disruption in membrane homeostasis, as no difference was detected in membrane tethered GFP (mCD8:GFP) expressed in wildtype and zyd cortex glia (Figure 1A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Western blot data.

claim: Cortex glial knockdown of Rab5 and EndoA completely suppressed zyd TS seizures.
source: In contrast, cortex glial knockdowns of Rab5, a Rab GTPase regulator of early endosome (EE) dynamics (Dunst et al., 2015; Langemeyer et al., 2018), and Endophilin A (EndoA), a BAR-domain protein involved in early stages of endocytosis (Verstreken et al., 2002), were found to be viable (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and to completely suppress zyd TS seizures (Figure 7A, Figure 7—video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data and citations.

claim: Adult flies conditionally expressing Rab5RNAi showed a partial rescue in zyd seizures, with only ~25% of flies showing HS-induced seizures.
source: Adult flies incubated for 16 hr at the restrictive temperature for gal80ts (31˚C) to allow Rab5RNAi expression, showed a partial rescue in zyd seizures, with only ~25% of flies showing HS-induced seizures (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: Adult flies and 3rd instar larvae conditionally expressing Rab5DN showed a partial rescue of zyd seizures with ~40% of animals displaying wildtype behavior.
source: Adult flies and 3rd instar larvae conditionally expressing Rab5DN showed a partial rescue of zyd seizures with ~40% of animals displaying wildtype behavior (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: Large (>0.1 μm2) Rab5-positive early endosomes accumulated in zyd cortex glia compared to controls.
source: We found that large (>0.1 μm2) Rab5-positive early endosomes accumulated in zyd cortex glia compared to controls (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by imaging data.

claim: Feeding zyd larvae the CN inhibitor, CsA (1 mM), restored the number of Rab5 compartments to control levels.
source: Feeding zyd larvae the CN inhibitor, CsA (1 mM), restored the number of Rab5 compartments to control levels (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by imaging data.

claim: Inhibition of endocytosis for 6 hr at 31 ˚C in zyd mutants co-expressing Shits suppressed the subsequent seizures observed during a 38.5˚C heat shock in ~80% of animals.
source: In contrast, inhibition of endocytosis for 6 hr at 31 ˚C in zyd mutants co-expressing Shits suppressed the subsequent seizures observed during a 38.5˚C heat shock in ~80% of animals (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: The seizure suppression observed after 6 hr of Dynamin inhibition was reversible, as adults tested 12 or 24 hr after return to room temperature regained the zyd seizure phenotype.
source: The seizure suppression observed after 6 hr of Dynamin inhibition was reversible, as adults tested 12 or 24 hr after return to room temperature regained the zyd seizure phenotype (Figure 7F, right).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: Pan-glial overexpression of sand:GFP partially suppressed zyd HS-induced seizures.
source: Indeed, pan-glial overexpression of sand:GFP partially suppressed zyd HS-induced seizures (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: Constitutive cortex glial overexpression of the open K+ channel EKO rescued vortex-induced seizures in ~75% of zyd mutants.
source: Constitutive cortex glial overexpression of the open K+ channel EKO (White et al., 2001) rescued vortex-induced seizures in ~75% of zyd mutants (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data and citation.

claim: Cortex glial overexpression of EKO led to a dramatic change in the behavior of ~60% of zyd animals during heat shock, showing partial recovery from the seizure phenotype to bottom dwelling and hypoactivity.
source: During a heat shock, cortex glial overexpression of EKO led to a dramatic change in the behavior of ~60% of zyd animals, showing partial recovery from the seizure phenotype to bottom dwelling and hypoactivity (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by behavioral data.

claim: CPG recordings revealed that zyd;NP2222>EKO larvae regain rhythmic muscle activity at 38.5˚C.
source: CPG recordings revealed that zyd;NP2222>EKO larvae regain rhythmic muscle activity at 38.5˚C (Figure 8D–E), indicating cortex glial K+ buffering is critical for neuronal excitability during states of intense excitation following heat shock or acute vortex.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: Cortex glial K+ buffering is critical for neuronal excitability during states of intense excitation following heat shock or acute vortex.
source: CPG recordings revealed that zyd;NP2222>EKO larvae regain rhythmic muscle activity at 38.5˚C (Figure 8D–E), indicating cortex glial K+ buffering is critical for neuronal excitability during states of intense excitation following heat shock or acute vortex.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the electrophysiology data.

claim: Enhanced CN-induced endocytosis leads to internalization and degradation of sand, impairment of cortex glial K+ buffering and increased seizure susceptibility in zyd mutants.
source: Together, these results indicate that enhanced CN-induced endocytosis lead to internalization and degradation of sand, impairment of cortex glial K+ buffering and increased seizure susceptibility in zyd mutants.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a summary interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Approximately 50 million people worldwide have epilepsy, making it one of the most common neurological diseases globally.
source: Approximately 50 million people worldwide have epilepsy, making it one of the most common neurological diseases globally (World Health Organization, 2018, http://www.who.int/en/).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to the WHO.

claim: Several anti-epileptic drugs reduce glial Ca2+ oscillations in vivo.
